steps.ttsScript: Hey there! Have you ever told someone about a really cool thing that happened to you?

We talk about the beginning, the middle, and the end. Let's learn how!

slides.heading: How Do We Retell a Story?

steps.ttsScript: Retelling a story is easy! You just think about what happened in order.
First, what happened at the beginning of the story?
Next, what happened in the middle?
And last, how did the story end? That's it! Beginning, middle, end. You've got this!
The middle is the biggest part of the story. It is everything that happens after the beginning, before the very end.
Say a puppy got lost at the start. In the middle, the puppy looks and looks for home. The middle holds the action! Always tell the middle, not just the beginning and end.
Here's a little story. Listen carefully!
A bird built a nest. Then she laid three eggs. At last, the baby birds hatched!

steps.ttsScript: Now let's retell it! What happened first? First, a bird built a nest!
What happened next? Next, she laid eggs!
And last? The babies hatched! You just retold a whole story! Amazing!
Here's a secret trick for retelling stories.
Use the magic words: first, next, and last. These words help you put everything in the right order!
Try it every time you hear a story. First this happened, next this, and last that!

steps.ttsScript: Grammar is the set of rules that helps us talk and write in a way that makes sense!
When we use good grammar, people understand us! And it's not hard at all.
Let's learn some basic grammar rules!
Did you know that words have different jobs? Some words name things — like 'cat' or 'ball.'
These are called nouns! A noun names a person, place, or thing.
Other words show action — like 'run,' 'jump,' or 'eat.' These are verbs!
Nouns and verbs work together to make sentences! Like: The cat runs.
Look at this sentence: The dog jumps.
What's the noun? The dog! Dog is a thing, so it's a noun!
What's the verb? Jumps! Jumping is an action, so it's a verb!
To find a noun, ask: Can I touch it or see it? If yes, it's probably a noun!
To find a verb, ask: Can I do it? If yes, it's a verb!
You're a grammar detective!

steps.ttsScript: Did you know that words can be related to each other? Like friends and family!
Some words are opposites — like 'hot' and 'cold.' Some words are similar — like 'happy' and 'glad!'

Opposites are words that mean the complete reverse. Big and small. Hot and cold. Up and down!
They're like two sides of a coin!
Words can also belong to groups. 'Dog,' 'cat,' and 'fish' are all animals!
And some words mean almost the same thing! 'Big' and 'large' are alike!

Sad! Happy and sad are opposites!

Connecting words to other words helps you remember them better!

steps.ttsScript: Fact books give us two kinds of clues.
The words tell us facts.
The pictures show us how it looks.
Today, we will learn how words and pictures give us different kinds of information in a book.

The picture shows us that ladybugs are red with black spots and have tiny legs.
So, the words gave us facts we can read, like what kind of animal it is.
And the picture gave us details we can see, like its color and shape.
Some things are hard to tell in words.
The exact color of an animal.
The shape of its spots. How tall it is.
Pictures show us those right away!
Sometimes, pictures and words in a book tell us different things.
Pictures often show us what something looks like or where it is.
Words can tell us names, feelings, or why something happened.
It's important to notice if the picture or the words are giving you new information.
You are now a pro at telling the difference between what pictures and words tell us!

steps.ttsScript: Listen! Every word is made of little sounds, hiding one right after another.
When we push those sounds together into one word, we call it blending.

Now push them together fast. Mmm-ooo-p. Mop!
You blended mmm, ooo, p into mop. Blending power!

steps.ttsScript: Prefixes change a word's meaning right at the start.
Take happy. Add un at the front. Now it's unhappy — meaning not happy!
Let's explore some common prefixes and see the power they have!
Unhappy. The un at the start means not. Unhappy means not happy.
Redo. The re at the start means again. Redo means do again.
Preview. The pre at the start means before. Preview means see before.
Disagree. The dis at the start means opposite. Disagree means not agree.
Misspell. The mis at the start means wrongly. Misspell means spell wrong.
Sub at the start means under. Submarine means under water.
Let's try one together. Here's a word.
Here is the word: dislike.
What is the prefix? DIS!
What does it mean? Not!
So dislike means not like. Prefix power!
Here is a helpful trick.
Peel the prefix. What is left is the root. Add the prefix's meaning back!
Prefix power!

steps.ttsScript: Every story is told by a narrator. The narrator decides whose eyes we see through.
Some narrators say 'I'. Others say 'he' or 'she'. And some can even read minds!
When the narrator says 'he' or 'she' but only knows ONE character's thoughts, that is third-person limited.
It is like following one person around. You hear only what that person feels.
When the narrator knows what EVERY character is thinking, that is third-person omniscient.
Omniscient means all-knowing. This narrator floats above and sees inside everyone.

steps.ttsScript: Does the narrator say I? No! It says Maya and Leo. So is it first or third person? Third!
Now, whose thoughts do we hear? We feel Maya's fear AND Leo's hope. Two minds!
Two minds means all-knowing. So this is third-person omniscient. You did it!
Here is a handy trick to remember.
Count the minds you can read. One mind is limited. Every mind is omniscient.

steps.ttsScript: Most words you can sound out. But a few are sneaky!

steps.ttsScript: A pronoun is a short word that stands in for a noun, like she, he, it, or they.
The noun the pronoun stands for is called the antecedent.
Today we make the pronoun agree with its antecedent.

More than one is plural. Use they or them.
